_comment: Production series, film 4: slides and a short run in FreeXmlToolkit (FundsXmlProdGeneratingDocVideo) on a file written by the generator of the complete example github.com/fundsxml/examples/tree/main/PostgreSQL_End_to_End (EXAMPLE-AM-INSURER-A-2025-11-05*.xml).

description.en: How to produce FundsXML from a database, with the generator of the complete PostgreSQL example: start with the target file, a mapping table, a partner register that says which data goes to whom, templates, XSLT or generated code, ControlData, writing share classes, several funds and dates in one file, element order, empty elements and formats, validation in FreeXmlToolkit, corrections, large deliveries, several schema versions, partner configuration, time windows, golden files, CI and the round trip, handing over, resends and documentation. All files can be downloaded.

say.en: Now the other direction: the data is in your database, and a partner expects a FundsXML file. In this film you see the ways to generate FundsXML, the mapping behind it, how to serve several partners from one generator, and how to test the result. The generator of the complete example writes from the database of the last two films, and you can download all of it.

items.head: An official example file
items.text: Close to what the partner expects.

items.head: Agreed with the partner
items.text: Before the first line of code.

say.en: Start with the target, not with the code. Take an official example file that comes close to what your partner expects, for example one of the realistic samples in the FundsXML examples repository. It shows which elements a complete delivery uses, in which order. Agree it with your partner, and you know what to build before the first line of code. The complete example keeps the files its generator must produce right next to the code.

en.title: The mapping table
rows: new for every file, never reused
per date and nature; Amount per currency
only assets the file refers to
in force on the content date

say.en: Then the mapping: for each element, where does the value come from? A simple table does the job: the FundsXML path, the source in the database, and the rule, such as a conversion or a fixed value. This table is the most important document of the project. It is also what the business side reviews, long before any file exists. The example keeps it as a file of its own, next to the code.

Which data goes to whom? The partner register answers it: which funds a partner receives, which kinds of data, and which templates. In the example, the distributor receives the umbrella and the multi-asset fund, with three days of prices, the documents and the E M T and E E T. The insurer receives two funds with their portfolios and the T P T. Adding a fund for a partner is a change in the register, not in the code.

en.title: Three ways to write the file

items.head: Templates
items.text: XML written directly from the query results.

items.head: Generated code
items.text: Classes from the schema: JAXB, xsdata.

say.en: There are three common ways to write the file. Templates write the XML directly from the query results; simple and easy to read. X S L T transforms an intermediate XML, for example from the database, into FundsXML. And code generators create classes from the schema, with JAXB in Java or xsdata in Python; the code then fills objects and writes them out.

items.head: Templates
items.text: Small and medium deliveries; you see the XML.

items.head: XSLT
items.text: When the data is XML already.

items.head: Generated code
items.text: Type safety, but large code, regenerated for every version.

say.en: Which one fits? Templates suit small and medium deliveries and teams that like to see the XML. X S L T suits setups where the data is already XML. Generated code gives type safety, but the FundsXML schema is large, so the generated code is too, and it must be regenerated for every new version.

en.title: ControlData of every file
en.code:
def control_data(self):
    return el("ControlData",
              el("UniqueDocumentID", self.doc_id),        # new for every file, never reused
              el("DocumentGenerated", self.generated),     # now ...
              el("Version", "4.2.9"),
              el("ContentDate", self.until),               # ... and the day the data is valid for
              el("DataSupplier", el("SystemCountry", "AT"), el("Short", "EXAMPLE-AM"), ...),
              el("DataOperation", "AMEND" if self.amend_of else "INITIAL"),
              el("RelatedDocumentIDs", el("RelatedDocumentID", self.amend_of))
                  if self.amend_of else None,
              el("Language", "en"))

say.en: Every file begins with control data. Generate a new document ID for every file, never reuse one. The generation time is now; the content date is the date the data is valid for, which is usually earlier. Name the data supplier. And set the data operation: initial for a first delivery, amend for a correction, with the ID of the delivery it corrects.

en.title: The example generator: a share class
en.code:
put(xf, el("ShareClass",
           el("Identifiers", el("ISIN", isin)), el("Names", el("OfficialName", name)),
           el("Currency", ccy), el("CurrencyHedgedFlag", hedged),
           self.prices(sc_id),                          # every date and nature
           self.total_asset_values(fund_id, sc_id, self.dates),  # one Amount per currency
           self.distributions(sc_id),
           self.flows(sc_id, fund_id)))

def prices(self, sc_id):
    found = rows(...SELECT nav_date, currency, nature, nav_price, ... FROM price
                    WHERE share_class_id = %s AND nav_date = ANY(%s) AND <current, released>)
    return el("Prices", *[el("Price", el("ActionCode", "C"), el("NavDate", d), ...)
                          for d, c, n, v, s, r in found])

say.en: The example uses templates written in code. This part writes a share class: the identifiers, the name, the currency, then its prices for every date and nature, its net assets in every currency, its distributions and its flows. The values come from the tables you saw in the earlier films, current and released only. The order of the elements follows the schema exactly, because X S D sequences are strict.

en.title: One database, three partners, three files

say.en: From one database, the example writes three quite different files. The distributor's file has an umbrella with two subfunds and a single fund, nine share classes, three days of prices with an estimated and an official value each, and no portfolio. The insurer's file has two funds with their month-end portfolios and the one hundred seventy-seven assets they hold. The data vendor gets everything.

en.title: Several funds and dates in one file

say.en: Several funds and dates in one file need no special code either. The generator writes one fund at a time, and forgets it when it is done. An umbrella brings its subfunds, found through the parent column, and each subfund its share classes. Every date and nature becomes one total asset value. The assets the positions refer to are collected on the way, and written once, at the end.

The order matters more than many expect. Here two elements of a share class were written the wrong way round. The schema does not accept it: the validator reports invalid content, and names the element it expected instead. The fix is in the generator, which must follow the sequence of the schema exactly, element by element.

en.title: Leave out what you do not have
en.code:
def el(tag, *content, **attrib):
    """An element, or None when it has no content: leave out what you do not have."""
    children = [c for c in content if isinstance(c, etree._Element)]
    values = [c for c in content if c is not None and not isinstance(c, etree._Element)]
    if not children and not values:
        return None
    ...

say.en: A rule that saves many errors: leave out what you do not have. An empty element is not the same as a missing one, and it often fails validation. Never write placeholders such as N A or zero. In the example, the one function that builds every element returns nothing when there is no value, so an empty element cannot be written at all. And if a required element has no value, the problem is in the data; fix it there.

Formats are the next source of trouble. Numbers use a decimal point and no thousands separators, whatever the language settings of the server. Dates are written year, month, day. Booleans are true or false. The file is U T F eight. And percentages are plain numbers, without a percent sign.

Here is the generated file for the insurer, opened in FreeXmlToolkit. Validation against the schema: valid. The data-quality check: no errors. Every generated file goes through exactly these checks before it leaves the house, automatically.

en.title: Generating a correction
en.code:
<ControlData>
  <UniqueDocumentID>EXAMPLE-AM-DATAVENDOR-C-2025-11-05-AMEND-1</UniqueDocumentID>
  <DocumentGenerated>2025-11-06T10:30:00</DocumentGenerated>
  <Version>4.2.9</Version>
  <ContentDate>2025-11-05</ContentDate>
  <DataSupplier>...</DataSupplier>
  <DataOperation>AMEND</DataOperation>
  <RelatedDocumentIDs>
    <RelatedDocumentID>EXAMPLE-AM-DATAVENDOR-C-2025-11-05</RelatedDocumentID>
  </RelatedDocumentIDs>
</ControlData>  ... then the complete corrected data for the funds and the date

say.en: Corrections are generated too. A correction is a new file with its own document ID, the data operation amend, and the ID of the delivery it corrects. It carries the complete corrected data for those funds and that date, not just the one changed number. Then the receiver can simply replace what it has, as you saw in the film about loading.

en.title: Large deliveries: a stream
en.code:
with etree.xmlfile(str(out), encoding="UTF-8") as xf:
    xf.write_declaration()
    with xf.element("FundsXML4", ...):
        xf.write(self.control_data())
        with xf.element("Funds"):
            for fund_id in self.top:            # one fund at a time
                self.write_fund(xf, fund_id)

def stream(conn, sql, *params):                 # positions: a server-side cursor
    with conn.cursor(name="export_stream") as cur:
        cur.itersize = 500; cur.execute(sql, params); yield from cur

say.en: For large deliveries, write the file as a stream too: with the XML stream writer in Java, or incremental writing in Python, as here. The example writes one fund at a time, and reads the positions through a server-side cursor, a few hundred rows at a time, so that memory stays small. Very large deliveries can be split, for example one file per fund. And compress the file for transport.

items.head: One generator
items.text: Differences in a table, not a copy.

say.en: Partners expect different versions. Keep one generator and describe the differences between the versions in a table, rather than copying the whole generator. New elements in FundsXML are usually optional, so a newer version mostly adds fields. Test every version you deliver, against its own schema.

items.head: No copy of the generator per partner

say.en: Partners have wishes: one wants the E S G template, another only some share classes, a third no documents. Handle these in configuration, not in code. The register says which blocks and templates each partner gets, and the generator follows it; in the example, the distributor gets documents and the insurer does not. A copy of the generator per partner is the fastest way into the trouble you saw in the first film of this series.

Generation usually has a short time window: between the approval of the data in the evening and the cut-off time of the partners. Generate funds in parallel, one fund per task. Start each delivery as soon as its data is approved, not at a fixed late hour. And measure how long it takes, so that you notice early when growth makes it too slow.

say.en: Test with golden files: a fixed set of input data and the file it must produce. In the example, the six deliveries are the input, and the four expected files are the output. After every change, the generator runs again, and the result is compared with the golden file, then validated and checked. Include the difficult cases: a correction, an umbrella, a share class in a second currency.

Automate the tests. In the example, every change runs through the same steps on GitHub: start the database, load the deliveries, reject the broken ones, generate the files for every partner, validate them, compare them with the golden files, and run the data-quality checks. A change that breaks the output is noticed before it reaches a partner.

say.en: One more test is cheap and finds a lot: load the generated file again, with the loader of the last film. Every asset must be found again: by its I S I N, or, for assets without one, by the key the generator wrote as other identifier. In the log, the four hundred thirty assets are all known: not one new asset is created. And every portfolio still reconciles to the cent.

After the checks, the file is handed over. It gets the agreed name, is compressed if it is large, and goes out on the agreed channel. Where possible, the receiver confirms that it arrived. And the file goes into the archive, together with its validation result, so that it can always be found again by its document ID.

items.head: Never regenerate it silently
items.text: The data may have changed since.

items.head: Changed content
items.text: Is a correction, with a new ID.

say.en: Sometimes a partner asks for a file again. Send the archived file, unchanged and with the same document ID. Do not generate it again from the database, because the data may have changed since, and the partner would receive different numbers under the same ID. If the content has to change, that is a correction, with a new ID.

items.head: Mapping table next to the code
An example file for every kind of delivery

say.en: Finally, document the generator. Keep the mapping table next to the code and change both together. Keep a short change log for your partners: what changed in the deliveries, and from when. And keep one example file for every kind of delivery; the golden files are exactly that. When a partner asks how a field is filled, the answer is found in minutes.

items.head: data/expected
items.text: The files for the three partners.

items.head: run_all.sh
items.text: Load, generate, validate, compare, load again.

say.en: Everything you saw in this film is in the complete example: the generator, the partner register, the mapping table, and the files it writes for the three partners. You find it in the FundsXML examples repository on GitHub, in the folder PostgreSQL end to end, also as a single zip file. Change the register, run the script, and compare your own files.

That was generating FundsXML: the target first, a clear mapping, a partner register, careful formats, and automatic tests with golden files and a round trip. In the last film of this series, you see how to run all this in daily operations. Thanks for watching.
